title: Chest radiograph — PA
summary: The film you will read more than any other: silhouettes, not structures.
text:
A posteroanterior film: the beam passes from back to front with the patient's chest against the detector, so the heart – close to the detector – is magnified as little as possible. The patient's right is on your left.

What you see is not organs but the edges where tissues of different density meet. The heart border is visible only because air-filled lung lies against it. Lose the air and you lose the line: that is why consolidation, collapse and effusion all announce themselves as a silhouette that has gone missing.

The model beside it is set up the same way – lungs, heart and great vessels solid, the ribcage left translucent, the way the beam sees them.
reading: Check it is adequate: the medial ends of the clavicles equidistant from the spine (rotation), ten posterior ribs visible (inspiration), and the vertebrae faintly visible through the heart (penetration).
Trachea central, then the mediastinal contours in order: right paratracheal stripe and SVC, right atrium, then aortic knuckle, pulmonary trunk, left ventricle.
Hila: the left is normally 1–2 cm higher than the right, because the left pulmonary artery arches over the left main bronchus.
Both hemidiaphragms sharp, right about 2 cm higher than left because of the liver, and both costophrenic angles crisp.
Then the lung fields zone by zone, comparing left with right, and finally the bones and soft tissues.

title: Chest radiograph — lateral
summary: The second view that turns a shadow into a place.
text:
Anterior is to the left of the image, posterior to the right. A lateral adds the third dimension the PA cannot give: whether a shadow lies in front of or behind the fissures, whether the retrosternal space is filled, and how deep the posterior costophrenic recess is.

Two clear spaces matter. The retrosternal space should be dark – filled means an anterior mediastinal mass or right ventricular enlargement. The retrocardiac space should also be dark – filled means a left lower lobe problem.
reading: Anterior on the left, posterior on the right; the arms are raised so the humeri are out of the way.
Follow the trachea down: it should run posteriorly, and the posterior wall is a thin line.
The retrosternal clear space, then the retrocardiac space, then the posterior costophrenic recess – the lowest point of the pleural cavity, and the first to fill with fluid.
The vertebral bodies should get progressively clearer as you move down; a sudden increase in density is a lower lobe problem.

title: Hand — dorsopalmar
summary: Eight carpal bones in two rows, and the order you must know them in.
text:
A left hand. Two rows of four carpal bones: from the thumb side, scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform proximally and trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate distally – Some Lovers Try Positions That They Cannot Handle.

The bone to look at hardest is the scaphoid: its blood supply enters distally and runs backwards, so a proximal fracture starves the proximal pole. Up to a quarter of scaphoid fractures are invisible on the first film, which is why a tender snuffbox is immobilised and re-imaged rather than discharged.
reading: Three smooth, parallel arcs should be traceable across the carpus (Gilula's lines); a step in any of them means a carpal dislocation.
Joint spaces should all be about 2 mm and even; widening of the scapholunate space beyond 3 mm is the Terry Thomas sign of a scapholunate tear.
Follow each metacarpal from base to head, then every phalanx – the fifth metacarpal neck is the commonest fracture in the hand.
Finally the soft tissues and the alignment of the carpal rows on the lateral view.

title: Knee — AP
summary: Two condyles on a plateau, and the joint space that tells you about the cartilage.
text:
A right knee. The film shows bone; almost everything that goes wrong with a knee – menisci, cruciates, cartilage – is invisible on it. What the film does show is alignment, joint space (a surrogate for cartilage thickness) and fractures.

The patella is superimposed on the femur in this projection, so it is assessed on a lateral or skyline view.
reading: Joint space: compare medial with lateral. Narrowing with subchondral sclerosis and osteophytes is osteoarthritis, and the medial compartment usually goes first.
Trace both cortical outlines of femur, tibia and fibula for a break in the line.
A lipohaemarthrosis – a fat–fluid level in the suprapatellar pouch on a horizontal-beam lateral – means an intra-articular fracture even if you cannot see the fracture.
In a child, check the physes; a Salter–Harris injury can look almost normal.

title: Hip — AP
summary: The film you read at 3 a.m., and the lines that make an occult fracture visible.
text:
A right hip. The femoral head sits in the acetabulum; the neck runs up and medially at about 125 degrees to the shaft.

The reason this film matters so much is the blood supply. Retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery run up the neck beneath the capsule, so an intracapsular fracture tears them and the head dies. That single fact decides the operation: replace an intracapsular fracture, fix an extracapsular one.
reading: Trace Shenton's line – a smooth curve from the medial femoral neck onto the inferior border of the superior pubic ramus. A step in it means a fractured neck of femur or a dislocated hip.
Compare the two sides for the neck–shaft angle and for shortening or external rotation (the lesser trochanter becomes more prominent).
Follow the cortex of the neck, both trochanters and the acetabular rim.
Check the joint space and the sourcil – the dense weight-bearing roof of the acetabulum.

title: Cervical spine — lateral
summary: Three lines, seven vertebrae, and the one you must see to call it adequate.
text:
Anterior is to the left. A lateral cervical spine is read along three smooth lines – the anterior vertebral, posterior vertebral and spinolaminar lines. Any step in them is significant until proved otherwise.

It is only adequate if you can see the whole of C7 and the top of T1: the cervicothoracic junction is where injuries hide.
reading: Adequacy: C1 to the top of T1 visible.
Alignment: the three lines, each a smooth lordotic curve.
Bones: the height and cortex of every body, the dens and its relation to the anterior arch of C1 (the atlanto-dental interval, under 3 mm in an adult).
Cartilage: disc spaces of even height.
Soft tissues: the prevertebral space – under about 7 mm at C2 and under 22 mm at C6; widening means haematoma.

title: CT abdomen — axial, liver and spleen
summary: One slice at T11/12, and the habit of orientation that makes CT readable.
text:
An axial slice, seen as if from the patient's feet: the patient's right is on your left, anterior is at the top, posterior at the bottom. This one is at about the level of T11/T12, where the liver, stomach and spleen sit under the diaphragm.

CT gives you density in Hounsfield units: air about −1000, fat around −80, water 0, soft tissue 30–70, acute blood 50–80, bone and contrast several hundred and up. The window you look through decides what you can see at all, which is why the same slice is reviewed on soft-tissue, lung and bone settings.

The 3D view beside it is cut in the same plane at the same level, and every structure the plane passes through is named around the edge of it.
reading: Fix the orientation first: patient's right on your left, anterior up.
Then work by compartment rather than by eye-catching abnormality: solid organs, hollow viscera, vessels, retroperitoneum, bones, body wall.
Follow the aorta and IVC down through the slices – they are your fixed landmarks, and their calibre and position tell you a great deal.
Compare left with right for the paired structures: kidneys, psoas, paraspinal muscles, ribs.
